title: The Emergence of Filipino Nationalism
subtitle: How thousands of islands started thinking of themselves as one country.
objectives: Explain what nationalism means and how a nation differs from a state
Identify the economic and educational causes of Filipino nationalism
Explain how the opening of the Suez Canal sped up the spread of ideas
Describe the colonial social classes and the place of the indio
Explain the secularisation controversy and the role of Father Jose Burgos
Describe the Cavite Mutiny of 1872 and the execution of GomBurZa

cards.title: Nobody is born knowing they are Filipino
cards.text: In 1800 these islands held dozens of peoples speaking different languages. Nothing made them one nation yet. This week is how that changed.

cards.title: You have already felt this
cards.text: When Pacquiao fought, police reported the streets going quiet. Strangers with nothing else in common became one thing for an hour.
points: **That feeling has a name.** It is nationalism.
**It is loyalty to your own nation**, not to a ruler.
**In 1800 nobody here had felt it yet.**

cards.title: What nationalism actually means
cards.text: Nationalism is the belief that you belong to a nation, and that the nation should govern itself.
points: **A nation** is a people who share a history and an identity.
**A state** is the government that rules a territory.
**Spain ruled the state.** Filipinos began to feel like a nation.
**Nationalism grows when those two stop matching.**

cards.title: Death Stranding is a game about this problem
cards.text: The whole game is linking isolated places into one network. Before you connect them they are separate shelters. Afterwards they are a country.
points: **7,641 islands, dozens of languages** — separate shelters.
**Ships, schools and newspapers** were the connection.
**A nation is a network** before it is ever a flag.

options: Believing your people are a nation that should govern itself
Believing your country should have the strongest army
Believing every country should be ruled by a king
question.explain: It is the belief that you belong to a nation, and that the nation should govern itself.

cards.title: The ports opened, and money changed everything
cards.text: Manila was opened to world trade in 1834. Sugar, hemp and tobacco poured out, and a new kind of Filipino got rich.
points: **Before that**, Spain controlled who was allowed to trade here.
**After 1834** Filipino farmers and traders sold to the world.
**That money bought something dangerous to Spain:** education.

cards.title: The ilustrados — the enlightened ones
cards.text: Wealthy Filipino families sent their sons to university in Manila, then in Europe. They came home with law degrees and dangerous ideas.
points: ***Ilustrado*** is Spanish for *enlightened*.
**The 1863 education decree** made primary school free and compulsory.
**More Filipinos could read Spanish** — and read what liberals wrote.
**Spain had trained its own opposition.**

cards.title: A shortcut that carried ideas
cards.text: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. It cut a new route through Egypt, and Spain suddenly got much closer.
points: **Roughly three months by sea became roughly one.**
**Students, newspapers and books** moved at the new speed.
**Change the route and you change who arrives.**
**Same reason a new rail line decides which towns matter.**

question.text: Why did the Suez Canal matter to Filipino nationalism?
options: It made travel and news between Europe and the Philippines far faster
It let Spain send soldiers overland instead of by sea
It gave the Philippines its own trade route to America
question.explain: It cut the journey from about three months to about one. Liberal ideas arrived far faster.

cards.title: Educated, and still called indio
cards.text: A Filipino could earn a law degree and still be treated as lesser. Spaniards used *indio* for anyone born here.
points: **Peninsulares** — Spaniards born in Spain. Top of everything.
**Insulares** — Spaniards born here. A step below them.
**Indios** — native Filipinos. Bottom, whatever they achieved.
**Nothing sharpens an identity** like being told it is lesser.

cards.title: They took the word
cards.text: *Filipino* first meant a Spaniard born in the islands. The ilustrados took the word and used it for everyone born here.
points: **A word can be captured** and turned around.
**Rizal and his friends called themselves Filipinos** deliberately.
**Naming yourself** is the oldest move in storytelling.

question.text: Who did the word Filipino originally refer to?
options: Spaniards born in the Philippines
Native Filipinos only
Spanish priests sent out from Spain
question.explain: Spaniards born in the islands. The ilustrados claimed the word for everyone born here instead.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Causes done. Part 2 is 1872 — one year, two events, and the moment this stopped being an argument. Your place is saved.

cards.title: The year that made it personal
cards.text: Ideas move slowly. Then something happens that people refuse to forget, and it moves fast. For Filipino nationalism, that year was 1872.

cards.title: Tap through the road to 1872
cards.text: Five events, in order. Each one made the next one possible.

cards.title: One fair governor, then the opposite
cards.text: Governor-General Carlos Maria de la Torre arrived in 1869 and treated Filipinos as equals. He lasted two years.
points: **De la Torre** ended flogging and welcomed Filipinos to his palace.
**Rafael de Izquierdo** replaced him in 1871 and undid all of it.
**He promised to rule** with a crucifix in one hand and a sword in the other.
**Losing a freedom** angers people more than never having had it.

question.text: What changed when Izquierdo replaced de la Torre in 1871?
options: The liberal reforms were reversed and rule became harsher
Filipinos were given seats in the Spanish parliament
The Spanish friars lost control of the parishes
question.explain: He reversed the reforms. Losing freedoms you have already tasted is what pushed people over.

cards.title: Who gets to run a parish?
cards.text: Spanish friars held the wealthy parishes. Filipino priests were trained and ordained, then handed nothing. They asked, and were refused.
points: **Regular priests** belong to Spanish religious orders — the friars.
**Secular priests** answer to the local bishop. Many were Filipino.
**Father Jose Burgos** led the campaign to hand the parishes over.
**The friars argued Filipinos were unfit.** That was the real fight.

cards.title: The Cavite Mutiny
cards.text: Izquierdo cancelled the arsenal workers' exemption from tribute and forced labour. About two hundred soldiers and workers at Fort San Felipe revolted.
points: **It was over in two days.**
**A pay dispute**, not a revolution. That is the point.
**Spain called it a nationwide plot** anyway.
**That gave them the excuse** to arrest the priests.

cards.title: GomBurZa
cards.text: Three priests were executed by garrote at Bagumbayan. Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora had no part in the mutiny.
points: **Gomez was in his seventies.** The other two were in their thirties.
**No real evidence** was ever produced against them.
**Thousands watched.** It was meant to be watched.
**Spain meant it as a warning.** It worked as a beginning.

question.text: The three priests executed in 1872 were proven to have led the Cavite Mutiny.
question.explain: False. No real evidence was shown. A pay dispute was used as the excuse to remove them.

cards.title: A writer made sure nobody forgot
cards.text: Rizal was a boy of ten when it happened. Nineteen years later he dedicated *El Filibusterismo* to the three priests.
points: **He wrote that their guilt was never made clear.**
**A dedication is a small thing** that outlived an empire.
**Naming the dead** is how you keep them arguing.

cards.text: Spain wanted the executions to end the argument. Instead they handed Filipinos three names, one date, and a reason to stop asking politely.

terms.def: Loyalty to your own nation, and the belief that it should govern itself.
A nation is a people with a shared identity. A state is the government that rules a territory.
An educated Filipino of the late 1800s, often schooled in Europe. Spanish for 'enlightened'.
The Spanish term for a native-born Filipino. It was used as an insult.
A Spaniard born in Spain / a Spaniard born in the Philippines.
The campaign to hand parishes from the Spanish friars to Filipino secular priests.
Fathers Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, executed on 17 February 1872.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Nationalism** = one people, one nation, governing itself.
**Trade, schools and the Suez Canal** built the middle class.
**January 1872: the Cavite Mutiny.** February: GomBurZa.
**Spain's warning became the starting gun.**

options: Believing your people are a nation that should govern itself
Believing your ruler should be obeyed without question
Believing your country should trade only with its neighbours
Believing every country should have the same religion
quiz.explain: It is loyalty to your own nation, plus the belief that the nation should rule itself.
quiz.objective: Explain what nationalism means and how a nation differs from a state

quiz.text: What did opening Manila to world trade in 1834 lead to?
options: A wealthy Filipino middle class who could pay for education
The immediate end of Spanish rule
The closing of all the other Philippine ports
A ban on Filipinos owning land
quiz.explain: Trade made Filipino families rich. Rich families sent their sons to university, and that produced the ilustrados.
quiz.objective: Identify the economic and educational causes of Filipino nationalism

quiz.text: What word describes the educated Filipinos of the late 1800s?
quiz.explain: The ilustrados. The word is Spanish for 'enlightened', and most were schooled in Manila or Europe.
quiz.objective: Identify the economic and educational causes of Filipino nationalism

quiz.text: How did the Suez Canal help Filipino nationalism?
options: It cut the journey to Spain from about three months to about one
It let Filipino ships reach America without Spanish permission
It moved the Philippines closer to the equator
It ended Spain's control of Philippine trade
quiz.explain: Faster ships meant faster ideas. Students, letters, books and newspapers all arrived far sooner.
quiz.objective: Explain how the opening of the Suez Canal sped up the spread of ideas

quiz.text: Who did the word Filipino originally refer to?
options: Spaniards born in the Philippines
Native Filipinos born in the islands
Spaniards born in Spain
Chinese traders living in Manila
quiz.explain: Spaniards born here, the insulares. The ilustrados took the word and claimed it for everyone.
quiz.objective: Describe the colonial social classes and the place of the indio

quiz.text: What was the secularisation controversy about?
options: Whether Filipino priests could run parishes instead of Spanish friars
Whether the Philippines should have any religion at all
Whether Mass could be said in Tagalog
Whether priests should be allowed to marry
quiz.explain: Filipino secular priests wanted the parishes held by Spanish friars. Father Jose Burgos led that campaign.
quiz.objective: Explain the secularisation controversy and the role of Father Jose Burgos

quiz.text: The Cavite Mutiny of 1872 began as a protest over lost pay and work exemptions.
quiz.explain: True. Izquierdo removed the arsenal workers' exemption from tribute and forced labour, and they revolted.
quiz.objective: Describe the Cavite Mutiny of 1872 and the execution of GomBurZa

quiz.text: Put these four events in the order they happened.
quiz.explain: 1834, then 1869, then January 1872, then February 1872. Each one made the next possible.
quiz.objective: Describe the Cavite Mutiny of 1872 and the execution of GomBurZa

quiz.text: Why were the executions of GomBurZa so important?
options: They convinced educated Filipinos that Spain would never treat them fairly
They started a war that Spain lost within a year
They forced Spain to give the parishes to Filipino priests
They ended the Spanish practice of using the word indio
quiz.explain: Spain executed three respected priests without real evidence. Reform through loyalty stopped looking possible.
quiz.objective: Describe the Cavite Mutiny of 1872 and the execution of GomBurZa

quiz.text: What single name is given to the three priests executed on 17 February 1872?
quiz.explain: GomBurZa, from Gomez, Burgos and Zamora. The name itself is how Filipinos kept them together.
quiz.objective: Describe the Cavite Mutiny of 1872 and the execution of GomBurZa

quiz.text: What was a Spaniard born in the Philippines called?
options: An insular
A peninsular
An indio
An ilustrado
quiz.explain: An insular. A peninsular was born in Spain, and an indio was a native-born Filipino.
quiz.objective: Describe the colonial social classes and the place of the indio

quiz.text: Which sentence describes the difference between a nation and a state?
options: A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state is a government ruling a territory
A nation is smaller than a state, and always part of one
A nation has a king; a state has a president
They mean the same thing in every case
quiz.explain: Spain ruled the state. Filipinos were starting to feel like a nation. Nationalism grew in that gap.
quiz.objective: Explain what nationalism means and how a nation differs from a state

teacher.summary: Week 2 covers the emergence of Filipino nationalism, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It is built as one causal chain rather than a list of dates: trade money produced an educated class, the Suez Canal accelerated the ideas that class was reading, racial ranking gave them a grievance, and 1872 turned that grievance into a cause. The interactive timeline card carries the chain visually, so the sequence can be recovered without re-reading the text. GomBurZa is handled plainly and without gore; the emphasis is on the absence of evidence, not on the method of execution.
discussion: Ask him to explain the difference between a nation and a state using the Philippines in 1872. If he can do that, the rest of the term gets easier.
Ask what Spain could have done differently in February 1872. It tests whether he understood that the executions backfired.
Ask why faster ships mattered so much. The point is that ideas travelled at the speed of the fastest transport available.
Ask who benefited from calling educated Filipinos 'indios'. It moves him from remembering the word to seeing what it was for.
teacher.extension: Have him draw the road to 1872 as a five-step chain from memory, writing one sentence under each step explaining what it made possible. Insisting on the 'made possible' sentence is what turns a memorised timeline into an argument.
misconceptions: 'The Cavite Mutiny was a revolution.' It was a workplace protest of about two hundred men, put down in two days. Spain chose to describe it as a plot.
'GomBurZa were executed for leading the mutiny.' No real evidence was ever produced. They were prominent in the secularisation campaign, which is the likelier reason.
'Filipino always meant native Filipinos.' It first meant Spaniards born in the islands. The ilustrados deliberately took the word.
'Nationalism means hating other countries.' It means believing your nation should govern itself. That is what the Term 1 topics are about.
